record.field: The wizard that creates and computes one batch of draft payslips for a division and a period.
Check the configuration and the eligible headcount in the scope panel, then compute. Computing creates drafts only — nothing is paid, sent or approved.
Every pay run on one board, in the column of the approval stage it is waiting at.
Your division on this demo is {{live:division_name}}, and its June run is at {{live:june_run_state}} right now. Look at "Awaiting your approval" first — that count is the work only you can unblock.
Look at "Awaiting your approval" first — that count is the work only you can unblock. Everything else on this board is somebody else's gate.
Line-by-line review of every payslip in one run, with the working behind each net figure.
Filter to "Need review" and read those first. A flag is the engine asking a question, not telling you something is broken.
Where attendance, overtime and HR data arrive from files and connected systems, before any of it becomes a payslip.
Start an import to use the guided flow — it scores the file and lets you fix rows before anything is written. A batch that stops before commit has changed nothing.
The four-step import: choose a source, review what matched, fix what did not, then commit.
Resolve every row in "Need attention" before you commit. Commit is the first control in this flow that writes anything — everything before it is a preview.
Final settlement for departing employees: last salary, unused leave and deductions, in one place.
Check that everyone settled here is excluded from the normal monthly run for the same period. A leaver in both is paid twice.
The audit trail behind every part-month amount: days worked, standard days, and the factor between them.
Read the factor, not the money. If the factor is right and the amount still looks wrong, the problem is upstream in the contract or the import.
Corrections that belong to a closed month, paid in the current one, with the source period recorded against them.
Check the source period on each line. That field is what lets a closed month stay closed and still be reported correctly later.
The visible rulebook: every payslip line for one division, as a named component with a formula you can read.

Read the component list first, then open the one behind the number you are asking about. Nothing here is live until a configuration is activated — and a simulation against last month is what tells you whether it should be.
The legacy Odoo salary structures and their rules — kept because historical payslips still reference them.
Read, do not build. New pay logic belongs in a formula configuration; what is here exists so that payslips from before the migration can still be explained.
The company's active insurance policy and tax table: BHXH, BHYT and BHTN rates and ceilings, and the thuế TNCN bands.

Check that the rates on display are the ones currently in force — the table shows the active policy with the latest effective date. To change one, create a new policy record dated from the day the change applies; never edit the one in force.
The connectors payroll data arrives through — an HR system, a time clock, the bank — with their field mappings and sync history.

Read the last-sync time on every connector, not just its status. Connected describes the credentials; the sync time describes the data, and a connector that stopped looks exactly like one that is working.
The command centre: the live run, four numbers that describe the company, and a card for each part of the product worth opening today.

Read the line under your name first — it names the live run and how much of it is still waiting. Then open the section the work is actually in; nothing on this screen is a second way of doing anything.
Every submitted run in the lane of the gate it is waiting at, with the net at stake across all of them.
Read the count in the header — that is the part of this queue only you can move. Then open the run rather than deciding from its card: the total is on the card and the flags are on the payslips.
The people roster: contract status, the monthly wage bill, and whether each person can actually be paid.
Filter to the people who are not payroll-ready and clear them before the run, not after it. Somebody with no bank account computes perfectly and is still not paid.
Every contract with its type, its period and its wage — the agreements payroll is actually computed from.
Read the expiring filter before the run. A contract that ends mid-month is a proration nobody asked for, and one still in draft pays nothing at all.
Executive analytics from the stored per-run roll-ups: the cost story, the department leaderboard, the statutory split and the analytics snapshots.

Read the state chip beside the headline before you quote it — the hero is the latest run whatever state it is in, while the leaderboard below waits for a done one. Then compare cost per head rather than total against total: headcount moves between months, and one more employee explains most of what looks like a rise.
A question builder over derived fact tables that reconcile to the payslip lines: one measure, one breakdown, the filters that scope them — and a waterfall that explains a movement.

Choose the measure before the filters — most wrong answers here are the right filter on the wrong measure. And quote the tags with the number: the same measure with one tag removed is a different figure that looks identical in an email.
The same months read as people: headcount paid, joiners and leavers, attendance exceptions and cost per head.
Read the headcount line as employees PAID, not employed. A step in it is a joiner wave, a leaver wave — or a run that left somebody out, which is the one worth checking.
The statutory filings this company's country asks for, grouped by authority and prefilled for one month.
Check that the month's runs have all reached done before you generate anything. The tiles read what has been computed, so an unfinished run is a filing that is short.
